title: The freshness tax
summary: One product change can leave several sets of instructions out of date. Reducing that maintenance starts with deciding which knowledge belongs in documents and which can come from the product.
body_markdown:
Move a setting to a different menu and the product is updated as soon as the release goes out. The help article, onboarding tour, and demo script still need someone to change them. Each contains its own account of how the product works.


That repeated maintenance is the freshness tax. A[knowledge base](https://frigade.com/glossary/knowledge-base) article may take only a few minutes to edit, but someone has to find it, check the new behavior, and remember where else those instructions appear.


## Why it compounds


Consider a change to team invitations. Suppose workspace owners can now invite people from a new Members page, while admins need an owner's approval. The release changes both the steps and who can complete them.


Updating the screenshot fixes part of the help article. The text also needs the new permission rule. An onboarding[tour](https://frigade.com/glossary/product-tour) may need a different audience, and a sales demo recorded with an admin account may no longer work as shown.


Each copy has an owner with a different reason for maintaining it. Support wants a reliable answer to send customers. Product wants new users to finish setup. Sales wants to explain the workflow in a demo. They all need to check the same change before updating their version.


A release checklist is useful here. It can name the affected content and assign the work. But adding a checklist does not reduce the number of places where the workflow has been copied. The next permission change creates the same work again.


## The structural fix


Start by separating instructions that describe the interface from information the interface cannot explain.


Where to invite a teammate is something an agent can learn by navigating the product. Why an organization restricts invitations, which roles it recommends, and when someone should contact support are things your team needs to explain. Both belong in a useful answer.


We built Frigade to[learn workflows from the product](https://frigade.com/features/always-accurate) alongside the documentation you connect. It signs in with the access you provide, learns how tasks work, and refreshes that knowledge on subsequent learning passes. You can schedule those passes or request an extra sync after a release.


There is still work to do. Someone needs to give the agent appropriate access, maintain the policies, and check its answers. The opportunity is to reduce how often that work includes rewriting the same sequence of clicks.


## What this looks like in practice


Take one workflow that changes often and list where you explain it today. For the invitation example, that might include a help article, a welcome tour, and a saved support reply.


Keep the content that contributes something beyond the steps. The article can explain roles, and a welcome message can help someone decide whom to invite. A saved reply that only repeats navigation steps may be a better candidate for the assistant to handle when a customer asks.


Test that assistance with the accounts it needs to support. An owner completing the task successfully does not tell you whether an admin gets the right explanation. After the next release, refresh the agent's knowledge and repeat the check before retiring any instructions customers still need.


This gives you a way to evaluate the change. Record which content you still had to edit and which questions still needed a support reply. You can then judge whether product learning reduced the maintenance for that workflow.


## The asset version


A workflow learned from the product can contribute to answers and guided help wherever Frigade is used. That makes it worth checking the underlying product knowledge carefully: an incorrect permission rule can affect more than one answer, too.


Start with a workflow you expect to change again. If the next release leaves you with fewer instructions to rewrite and customers can still complete the task, expand from there.


## What is the freshness tax in product documentation?


The freshness tax is the work of keeping help articles, tours, and other instructions aligned with a changing product. It includes finding affected content, checking the new behavior, and updating each copy of the instructions.
